set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Eye pain WITH HEADACHE suggests what?
opts: Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis pairs eye pain with a gritty feeling; eye pain with headache suggests acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Correct — eye pain together with headache is the pairing for acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Corneal abrasion or foreign body
A corneal abrasion or foreign body hurts with blinking; eye pain with headache suggests acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis causes pain on eye motion; eye pain with headache suggests acute narrow angle glaucoma.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 17

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: What is the pain of acute iritis like?
opts: Severe, aching, deep
Severe, aching, deep pain is glaucoma; the pain of acute iritis is moderate rather than severe.
Absent
Absent pain is subconjunctival hemorrhage; the pain of acute iritis is moderate, aching and deep.
Moderate, aching, deep
Correct — acute iritis causes moderate, aching, deep pain, along with decreased vision.
Mild discomfort rather than pain
Mild discomfort rather than pain is conjunctivitis; the pain of acute iritis is moderate, aching and deep.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Which nerve mediates the pupillary constriction of the near reaction?
opts: The oculomotor nerve; accompanied by convergence and accommodation
Correct — the oculomotor nerve mediates the near constriction; convergence and accommodation happen alongside it but are not part of it.
The optic nerve; accompanied by convergence and dilation
The oculomotor nerve, not the optic nerve, mediates the near constriction, and the pupils constrict rather than dilate.
The trochlear nerve; accompanied by depression and intorsion
The trochlear nerve does not mediate it; the near constriction, like the light reaction, is mediated by the oculomotor nerve, cranial nerve III.
The abducens nerve; accompanied by abduction
The abducens nerve does not mediate it, and the eyes converge rather than abduct; the near constriction is mediated by the oculomotor nerve.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 80

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Which of these belongs in the URGENT group, seen by ophthalmology within a day or less?
opts: Pinguecula and pterygium
A pinguecula is harmless, and neither is on the urgent list, which includes acute glaucoma and retinal detachment.
Acute glaucoma
Correct — acute glaucoma is on the urgent list with orbital cellulitis, corneal ulcer or abrasion, retinal detachment and hyphema.
Sudden vision loss, chemical burns and suspected globe rupture
Those are emergent complaints, referred to ophthalmology immediately rather than within a day.
Dry eye and blepharitis
Neither is on the urgent list, which includes acute glaucoma, orbital cellulitis, retinal detachment and hyphema.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 124

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Corneal injury, acute iritis and glaucoma can make the eye diffusely red rather than showing ciliary injection. Which clues still point to them?
opts: Pain, decreased vision, unequal pupils, a hazy cornea
Correct — pain, decreased vision, unequal pupils and a less than perfectly clear cornea mark these more serious disorders.
Itch, watery discharge and lid crusting
Itching and watery discharge point to allergic or viral conditions; the serious disorders show pain, poor vision and unequal pupils.
Bilateral involvement together with a tender preauricular node
Bilateral involvement and a preauricular node do not mark these disorders; pain, decreased vision, unequal pupils and a hazy cornea do.
Fever and periorbital swelling
Fever and periorbital swelling do not mark these disorders; pain, decreased vision, unequal pupils and a hazy cornea do.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: How is the static finger wiggle test performed?
opts: Covering and uncovering each eye in turn
Covering and uncovering each eye reveals slight muscle imbalance; it is not a visual field test.
Wiggling fingers brought slowly inward from beside the ears until seen
Correct — at arm's length, hands two feet apart beside the ears, wiggling fingers come slowly inward until seen, quadrant by quadrant.
Moving a red-topped pin inward from beyond the boundary of each quadrant
A red-topped pin moved in from each quadrant is the kinetic red target test, the static test's partner.
Shining a light alternately into each eye
Swinging a light between the eyes is the swinging light test of optic nerve function, not a field test.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 53

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Where does a chalazion usually point?
opts: At the lateral canthus
A chalazion does not point to the lateral canthus; it usually points inside the lid rather than on the lid margin.
Inside the lid rather than on the lid margin
Correct — a chalazion, a nodule of a blocked meibomian gland, usually points inside the lid rather than on the lid margin.
On the lid margin, right at the base of the lashes
The lid margin is where a hordeolum sits; a chalazion usually points inside the lid rather than on the margin.
At the medial canthus
The medial canthus is where the lacrimal sac is compressed; a chalazion usually points inside the lid, not at a canthus.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: At what setting can an ophthalmoscope be used to look for a corneal ulcer?
opts: Set at +40 diopters, giving roughly a ten times magnifier
Correct — +40 diopters in effect fixes a 10 times magnifying lens, though fluorescein staining is more sensitive for early ulcers.
Set at zero diopters — and this is more sensitive than fluorescein
The setting is +40 diopters, not zero, and fluorescein staining is more sensitive than the ophthalmoscope for early ulcers.
Set at minus 20 diopters — with fluorescein being less sensitive
The setting is +40 diopters, and fluorescein is the MORE sensitive test for early ulcers.
No ophthalmoscope setting is useful here
The ophthalmoscope at +40 diopters acts as a 10 times magnifier that may reveal the corneal ulcer.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 123

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Eye pain WITH BLINKING suggests what?
opts: Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Acute narrow angle glaucoma pairs eye pain with headache; pain with blinking suggests corneal abrasion or foreign body.
Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis causes pain on eye motion; pain with blinking suggests a corneal abrasion or foreign body.
Temporal arteritis
Temporal arteritis pairs eye pain with temporal pain; pain with blinking suggests a corneal abrasion or foreign body.
Corneal abrasion or a foreign body
Correct — eye pain with blinking points to a corneal abrasion or a foreign body on the eye's surface.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 17

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: A red eye with severe deep pain, a steamy cornea and a dilated fixed pupil signifies what?
opts: Bacterial, viral and other infections, or allergy and irritation
Infection, allergy or irritation is the significance of conjunctivitis, which has mild discomfort, a clear cornea and a normal pupil.
Abrasions and other injuries; viral and bacterial infections
Injuries and infections are the significance of corneal injury, where the pupil is unaffected unless iritis develops.
Often none; may result from trauma, bleeding disorders, or a sudden increase in venous pressure
That is subconjunctival hemorrhage, which is painless with a clear cornea and an unaffected pupil.
An acute increase in intraocular pressure — an emergency
Correct — severe deep pain, a steamy cornea and a fixed dilated pupil signify an acute rise in intraocular pressure, an emergency.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Acute, unilateral and PAINLESS visual loss suggests which group of causes?
opts: Simple glaucoma or cataract
Simple glaucoma or cataract causes GRADUAL painless loss, not the acute unilateral painless picture.
Retinal vascular occlusion, retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage, macular degeneration
Correct — acute, unilateral, painless loss suggests retinal vascular occlusion, retinal detachment, vitreous hemorrhage or macular degeneration.
Corneal abrasion or ulcer, uveitis, traumatic hyphema, acute narrow angle glaucoma
Those are the acute, unilateral PAINFUL causes, which usually sit in the cornea and anterior chamber.
Thermal, radiation or chemical exposure
Thermal, radiation or chemical exposure is considered when symptoms are acute, BILATERAL and painful.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 16

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Nodular episcleritis is associated with which two systemic diseases?
opts: Graves disease, myasthenia gravis and thyroid orbitopathy
Graves disease causes proptosis and myasthenia gravis ptosis; nodular episcleritis goes with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
Sjögren syndrome and sarcoidosis
Sjogren's syndrome causes dry mouth and dry eyes; nodular episcleritis goes with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus erythematosus
Correct — nodular episcleritis can be seen in rheumatoid arthritis and lupus erythematosus.
Diabetes and hypertension
Diabetes and hypertension show in the fundus, as retinopathy and hard exudates; nodular episcleritis goes with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 47

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Which cause of red eye has no discharge, an unaffected pupil, a clear cornea and no pain?
opts: Subconjunctival hemorrhage
Correct — subconjunctival hemorrhage has absent pain and discharge, an unaffected pupil and vision, and a clear cornea.
Uncomplicated bacterial conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis has watery, mucoid or mucopurulent discharge and mild discomfort, though its pupil and cornea are normal.
Acute iritis
Acute iritis has moderate aching pain and a pupil that may be small and irregular.
Glaucoma
Glaucoma has severe aching pain, a steamy cloudy cornea and a dilated fixed pupil.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: What must be documented when the pupils are dilated?
opts: The time of dilation and the agents used
Correct — record the time of dilation and the agents used; a weak mydriatic reverses in 4 to 6 hours.
The visual acuity before dilation only
Acuity is not what dilation requires you to record; document the time of dilation and the agents used.
The patient's consent form number
A form number is not what is recorded; document the time of dilation and the agents used.
Nothing specific
Dilation must be documented: record both the time of dilation and the agents used.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 99

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Which complaints fall in the EMERGENT group, referred to ophthalmology immediately?
opts: Sudden vision loss, retinal artery occlusion, chemical burns, rupture, acute angle-closure glaucoma, and vitreous hemorrhage
Correct — sudden vision loss, retinal artery occlusion, chemical burns, rupture, angle closure and vitreous hemorrhage go to ophthalmology immediately.
Acute glaucoma, orbital cellulitis, corneal ulcer or abrasion, retinal detachment, macular edema, and hyphema
Those are the urgent complaints, sent for ophthalmology follow-up in one day or less rather than immediately.
Blepharitis, chalazion and dry eye
None of these is on the emergent list, which includes sudden vision loss, chemical burns and globe rupture.
Conjunctivitis and subconjunctival hemorrhage
A subconjunctival hemorrhage is usually harmless, and neither is emergent; chemical burns and rupture are.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 124

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Bilateral visual loss usually implies which kind of problem?
opts: A primary neurologic cause rather than a primary ophthalmologic one
Correct — bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology and not a primary ophthalmologic problem.
A primary ophthalmologic cause rather than a neurologic one
It runs the other way: bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology, not an ophthalmologic one.
An infective cause
Infection is not the usual inference; bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology.
A traumatic cause
Trauma is not the usual inference; bilateral visual loss usually implies a primary neurologic etiology rather than an eye problem.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 10 (speaker notes)

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: When must pupillary reactions be checked, relative to dilation?
opts: After dilating
Pupillary reactions come before dilation in the suggested order, not after; a mydriatic's effect lasts 4 to 6 hours.
It makes no difference
Timing matters: pupillary reactions are checked before dilating, and the dilation lasts 4 to 6 hours.
Only after the fundoscopic examination
Fundoscopy is done after dilation outside primary care, so the pupils are checked before it, not after.
Before dilating
Correct — pupillary reactions are checked before dilating; the weak mydriatic used for fundoscopy takes 4 to 6 hours to reverse.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Once local eye disease is excluded, which of these remains a cause of a dilated pupil?
opts: Optic neuritis, papilledema and optic atrophy
Optic nerve disease affects the afferent limb; the remaining causes are a third nerve lesion, an Adie's pupil or pharmacologic block.
Compression or other lesion of the third cranial nerve
Correct — the three remaining causes are a third nerve lesion, ciliary ganglion damage causing Adie's pupil, and pharmacologic sphincter block.
Glaucoma, cataract and macular degeneration
Those are local eye diseases, already excluded; what remains is a third nerve lesion, an Adie's pupil or a pharmacologic block.
Horner syndrome, myasthenia gravis and Graves disease
Horner syndrome gives a SMALL pupil; what remains is a third nerve lesion, an Adie's pupil or a pharmacologic block.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 86

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Which two structures are commonly left unexamined?
opts: The eyelids and eyebrows
Lids and brows are not among the common omissions; the structures commonly missed are the cornea and lens.
The lacrimal sac and puncta
The lacrimal sac is not among the common omissions; the structures commonly missed are the cornea and lens.
The extraocular muscles
Eye movements are not among the common omissions; the two structures commonly missed are the cornea and lens.
The cornea and the lens
Correct — failure to examine the cornea and lens is one of the common mistakes in the eye examination.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 20

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: How does the SIZE of the striking object change the injury?
opts: Object size makes no difference
Size is important: it determines whether the periocular soft tissues or the globe itself is likely to be injured.
Only velocity matters, not size
Velocity matters for penetration, but size matters too: larger objects hit the orbital rim, smaller ones the globe.
Larger objects transfer most of the energy to the orbital rim
Correct — larger objects transfer most of their energy to the orbital rim, while smaller objects may strike the globe itself.
Larger objects strike the globe directly; smaller objects hit the orbital rim
This reverses the mechanics: smaller objects may strike the globe directly, while larger ones load the orbital rim.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 111

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Besides faulty alignment, what causes diplopia?
opts: Dry eye
Dryness belongs with lacrimal obstruction or Sjogren's syndrome; diplopia arises from faulty alignment or a neurological problem.
Cataract
Cataract is a lens opacity causing gradual painless loss; diplopia arises from faulty alignment or a neurological problem.
A neurological problem
Correct — besides faulty alignment, diplopia comes from neurological problems: brainstem or cerebellar lesions, or extraocular muscle weakness.
Refractive error alone, without a neurological component
Refractive error is what a pinhole corrects; diplopia arises from faulty alignment or a neurological problem.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: An acute, significantly dilated pupil is a medical emergency particularly when accompanied by what?
opts: Headache or other neurologic signs
Correct — with headache or neurologic signs, an acutely dilated pupil may mean uncal herniation or a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
Itching or discharge — from an allergic conjunctivitis
Itching and discharge point to allergy, which leaves the pupil unaffected; headache or neurologic signs make the dilated pupil an emergency.
Fever — from orbital cellulitis
Fever is not the warning pairing; an acutely dilated pupil is an emergency with headache or other neurologic signs.
Blurred vision alone — from cataract
Cataract is a lens opacity that does not dilate the pupil; headache or neurologic signs make a dilated pupil an emergency.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 73

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Which description of xanthelasma is accurate?
opts: At the lid margin — consider bacterial infection
A painful infection at the lid margin is a hordeolum; xanthelasma sit nasally on the lids and suggest lipid disorders.
On the bulbar conjunctiva — consider ultraviolet exposure
A yellowish nodule on the bulbar conjunctiva is a pinguecula; xanthelasma sit nasally on the lids and suggest lipid disorders.
Along the NASAL portions of one or both eyelids — consider lipid disorders
Correct — xanthelasma are raised yellowish plaques along the nasal portions of the eyelids that should prompt a look for lipid disorders.
Along the temporal portions of the lids — consider thyroid disease
The plaques sit on the nasal, not temporal, portions of the lids, and they point to lipid disorders rather than thyroid disease.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 34

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Purulent discharge suggests what?
opts: Viral conjunctivitis
Viral conditions give watery or mucoid discharge; purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection.
Dry eye
Dryness points to lacrimal obstruction or Sjogren's syndrome; purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection.
Bacterial infection
Correct — purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection, while watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergy or a virus.
Allergic conjunctivitis
Allergic conditions give watery or mucoid discharge; purulent discharge suggests a bacterial infection.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 19

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: How is a fluorescein stain performed?
opts: The dye stains intact epithelium and spares defects
It is the reverse: the dye is taken up by areas of cornea devoid of epithelium, lit with a blue light.
The dye is injected intravenously and photographed with a blue flash
The dye is placed in the eye, not injected; a blue light then shows foreign bodies or corneal damage.
The dye changes the color of the aqueous humor
The dye is placed on the eye and viewed under blue light, where areas of cornea without epithelium take it up.
Orange dye is instilled and a blue light used
Correct — orange dye goes into the eye and a blue light shows foreign bodies or corneal damage, since bare areas take up the dye.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 121

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: Which immunization status matters in eye trauma?
opts: Hepatitis B
Hepatitis B status is not the one tied to eye trauma; tetanus immunization status is what matters after an eye injury.
Tetanus
Correct — tetanus immunization status is important in any patient with a history of eye trauma.
Influenza
Influenza status is not the one tied to eye trauma; tetanus immunization status is what matters after an eye injury.
Pneumococcal
Pneumococcal status is not the one tied to eye trauma; tetanus immunization status is what matters after an eye injury.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 15

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: How do you assess whether the eyes are truly protruding?
opts: Palpate the globe to judge its forward position
The globe is not palpated, and it is critical not to in trauma; protrusion is judged by inspecting from behind and above.
Stand behind the seated patient and inspect from above
Correct — stand behind the seated patient, look down from above, and draw the lids up to compare the corneas with the lower lids.
Sit facing the patient and compare the two eyes directly
Prominent eyes are judged from behind and above the seated patient, comparing the corneas with the lower lids.
Shine a light from the temporal side and look for a shadow
Oblique light from the temporal side looks for the iris shadow of a narrow angle; protrusion is judged from behind and above.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 25

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: What happens when a mydriatic is instilled in an Argyll Robertson pupil?
opts: Full and rapid dilation
The dilation is incomplete, not full; mydriatics only partly dilate the small, irregular Argyll Robertson pupil.
No change at all
The pupil does respond, but incompletely; mydriatics cause an incomplete dilation of an Argyll Robertson pupil.
Paradoxical constriction
A mydriatic dilates rather than constricts; in an Argyll Robertson pupil the dilation is simply incomplete.
Incomplete dilation
Correct — mydriatics cause only an incomplete dilation of an Argyll Robertson pupil.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 84

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: When is globe rupture more likely in a patient with a subconjunctival hemorrhage?
opts: When the hemorrhage is small, flat and confined to one sector
A small patch is the usually harmless picture; rupture is more likely when the hemorrhage encircles the entire cornea after trauma.
When the patient is anticoagulated
A bleeding disorder can cause the hemorrhage, but rupture is signaled by trauma with blood encircling the entire cornea.
When both eyes are affected
Bilaterality is not the warning sign; rupture is more likely with trauma and hemorrhage encircling the entire cornea.
In trauma, and when the hemorrhage encircles the entire cornea
Correct — globe rupture is more likely after trauma and when the hemorrhage encircles the entire cornea.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set1.q: What is the vital sign of the eye?
opts: Pupil reactivity
Pupillary reactions are checked before dilating, but visual acuity is the one called the vital sign of the eye.
Visual fields
Visual field testing follows acuity in the order; visual acuity is the one called the vital sign of the eye.
Visual acuity
Correct — visual acuity testing is called the vital sign of the eye and comes early in the suggested order.
Intraocular pressure
Intraocular pressure is likened to systemic blood pressure, but visual acuity is the one called the vital sign of the eye.
set1.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: In a trauma patient, what must NOT be done?
opts: Do not take a history
The history still matters, including tetanus status and any chemical's acidity; what must not be done is palpating the globe.
Do not palpate the globe
Correct — in trauma it is critical not to palpate the globe, and too much pressure on a ruptured globe is a known mistake.
Do not measure visual acuity
Visual acuity is still tested in trauma, following the same pattern as a routine eye examination; the globe is not palpated.
Do not inspect the lids
The eyelids are still examined in trauma as part of the routine pattern; what must not be done is palpating the globe.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 24

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Which two tests together make up the best confrontation field examination?
opts: Tonometry and fundoscopy
Tonometry measures intraocular pressure and fundoscopy views the disc and retina; fields use the finger wiggle and red target tests.
The static finger wiggle test and the kinetic red target test
Correct — confrontation fields are best tested by combining the static finger wiggle test with the kinetic red target test.
The swinging light test together with the cover-uncover test
The swinging light test checks optic nerve function and cover-uncover muscle imbalance; fields use finger wiggle and red target.
The pinhole test and the Snellen chart
The pinhole and Snellen chart test visual acuity; confrontation fields use the finger wiggle and kinetic red target tests.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 53

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Which three features define Horner syndrome?
opts: A large slow pupil with reduced light reaction and a slow near reaction
A large pupil with slow light and near reactions is Adie's tonic pupil; Horner syndrome gives a small pupil with ptosis.
Ptosis, miosis of the affected eye, anhidrosis of the ipsilateral face
Correct — Horner syndrome gives ptosis, miosis and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis, and the small pupil still reacts to light and near.
Ptosis, mydriasis, lateral deviation, and a fixed pupil
A fixed dilated pupil with ptosis and lateral deviation is oculomotor palsy; Horner gives ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
Lid lag, proptosis, chemosis and diplopia
Lid lag and proptosis are hyperthyroid and Graves signs; Horner syndrome gives ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 88

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Entropion and ectropion both affect which eyelid?
opts: Neither — they affect the conjunctiva
They are lid malpositions, not conjunctival disease: entropion turns the lower lid in, ectropion turns it out.
The lower lid
Correct — entropion is inward folding and ectropion outward turning, and both affect the lower lid.
The upper lid
Both malpositions affect the lower lid: entropion folds it inward and ectropion turns it outward.
Both lids equally
They do not affect both lids equally; entropion and ectropion are both lower lid malpositions.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 3

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: What causes SENILE ptosis?
opts: Compression of the oculomotor nerve
Oculomotor damage is a separate ptosis cause; senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle, relaxed tissues and herniated fat.
Weakened muscle, relaxed tissues
Correct — senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle and relaxed tissues, plus the weight of herniated fat.
Antibody blockade at the neuromuscular junction of the levator
Myasthenia gravis is a separate cause of ptosis; senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle, relaxed tissues and herniated fat.
Interruption of the sympathetic supply
Sympathetic interruption causes Horner syndrome's ptosis; senile ptosis comes from weakened muscle, relaxed tissues and herniated fat.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 29

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Why may a zygomatic fracture cause pain on opening the mouth?
opts: The masseter originates on the mandible and inserts on the zygoma
The pain is explained by the temporalis, which passes medial to the arch and inserts on the mandible, not by the masseter.
The infraorbital nerve is compressed during jaw movement
Infraorbital nerve damage causes hypesthesia of the infraorbital area; mouth-opening pain comes from the temporalis under the arch.
The temporomandibular joint is always involved
The jaw joint is not the explanation; the temporalis passes medial to the zygomatic arch and inserts on the mandible.
The temporalis muscle passes medial to the arch and inserts on the mandible
Correct — the temporalis passes medial to the zygomatic arch and inserts on the mandible, so a fracture can hurt on opening.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 116

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Watery or mucoid discharge suggests which conditions?
opts: Acute glaucoma
Acute glaucoma produces no ocular discharge; watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergic or viral conditions.
Allergic or viral
Correct — watery or mucoid discharge goes with allergic or viral conditions, while purulent discharge suggests bacteria.
Bacterial infection
Bacterial infections produce purulent discharge; watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergic or viral conditions.
Acute iritis
Acute iritis produces no ocular discharge; watery or mucoid discharge suggests allergic or viral conditions.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 19

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: A temporal field defect in one eye should prompt what?
opts: Testing for a nasal defect in the other eye
Correct — a temporal defect in one eye may suggest a nasal defect in the other eye, so test that possibility.
Immediate fundoscopy of the same eye only
Fundoscopy is not the next step; a temporal defect in one eye may mean a nasal defect in the other, which should be tested.
Repeating acuity in the same eye
Acuity is not the next step; a temporal field defect in one eye should prompt testing the other eye for a nasal defect.
Measuring intraocular pressure
Pressure is not the next step; a temporal field defect in one eye should prompt testing the other eye for a nasal defect.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 55

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: What is interrupted in Horner syndrome?
opts: The oculomotor nerve
Oculomotor paralysis gives a dilated fixed pupil with lateral deviation; Horner syndrome is a sympathetic interruption.
The optic nerve
Optic nerve damage gives an afferent (Marcus Gunn) defect; Horner syndrome is a sympathetic interruption.
The sympathetic innervation of the pupil and the levator palpebrae superioris
Correct — interrupting sympathetic supply to the pupil and levator palpebrae superioris explains both the miosis and the ptosis.
The parasympathetic supply travelling through the ciliary ganglion
Parasympathetic loss at the ciliary ganglion produces Adie's tonic pupil; Horner syndrome is a sympathetic interruption.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 88

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: After a chemical or fluid splash to the eye, what must you establish?
opts: The manufacturer of the product
The brand is not what matters; the essential fact after a chemical exposure is its acidity or alkalinity.
The acidity or alkalinity of the fluid
Correct — after any chemical or fluid exposure, knowing whether the fluid was acidic or alkaline is essential.
The volume of fluid involved
Volume is not what must be known; you must establish whether the fluid or chemical was acidic or alkaline.
Whether the patient was wearing contact lenses
Contact lens wear is not the essential fact here; you must establish the acidity or alkalinity of the fluid.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 15

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Which two conditions are associated with blepharitis?
opts: Hypothyroidism and iron deficiency
Hypothyroidism shows as lateral eyebrow sparseness; blepharitis is associated with bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis.
Graves disease and myasthenia gravis
Graves disease causes proptosis and myasthenia gravis causes ptosis; blepharitis goes with bacteria and atopic dermatitis.
Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus
Rheumatoid arthritis and lupus go with nodular episcleritis; blepharitis goes with bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis.
Bacterial infection and atopic dermatitis
Correct — blepharitis is a common eye inflammation associated with bacterial infections and with atopic dermatitis.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: What is the rule about topical anesthetic in corneal abrasion?
opts: It should be prescribed for home use to control the pain
It is not a take-home treatment; topical anesthetic in abrasion is used for diagnosis only, despite the immediate relief.
It should never be used at all
It is used, but for diagnosis: topical anesthetic brings immediate relief of an abrasion and is not a treatment.
It is only useful if the cornea is hazy
A hazy cornea suggests bacterial infection; topical anesthetic is used for diagnosis of an abrasion, not treatment.
Use it for diagnosis, not as a treatment
Correct — topical anesthetic brings immediate relief of an abrasion, but it is used for diagnosis and not as a treatment.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 120

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Injection localized JUST AROUND THE CORNEA suggests which three conditions?
opts: Keratitis, iritis, or acute glaucoma
Correct — injection just around the cornea could result from keratitis, iritis or acute glaucoma.
Conjunctivitis, blepharitis, or dry eye
Conjunctivitis gives diffuse redness maximal peripherally, not a ring around the cornea; that ring suggests keratitis, iritis or glaucoma.
Subconjunctival hemorrhage, pinguecula, or pterygium
Those are localized patches or growths of the conjunctiva; injection just around the cornea suggests keratitis, iritis or acute glaucoma.
Episcleritis, chalazion, or hordeolum
Those are nodules and lid lesions; injection just around the cornea suggests keratitis, iritis or acute glaucoma.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 46

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: What is the warning about pressure on a globe that may be ruptured?
opts: Placing too much pressure on it is a mistake
Correct — failing to diagnose a ruptured globe and placing too much pressure on it are both common examination mistakes.
Pressure is required to assess the depth of injury
Pressure is not used to judge depth; placing too much pressure on a ruptured globe is itself a recognized examination mistake.
Pressure is harmless once a topical anesthetic has been instilled
Anesthetic does not make it safe; placing too much pressure on a ruptured globe is a recognized examination mistake.
Pressure should be applied only with a cotton swab
No instrument makes it safe; too much pressure on a ruptured globe is a recognized mistake, and the globe is not palpated in trauma.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Which cause of red eye shows redness that is DIFFUSE and maximal peripherally, with vision unaffected?
opts: Glaucoma
Glaucoma gives deep-vessel redness around the limbus, a steamy cloudy cornea, a dilated fixed pupil and decreased vision.
Corneal injury or infection
Corneal injury or infection gives deep-vessel redness around the limbus with vision usually decreased.
Conjunctivitis
Correct — conjunctivitis gives diffuse conjunctival redness maximal peripherally, with vision affected only by mild blurring.
Acute iritis
Acute iritis gives injection of the deeper vessels around the limbus and decreased vision.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Why does moving the light to the affected eye cause BOTH pupils to dilate in an afferent defect?
opts: The oculomotor nerve is being compressed on that side
Oculomotor compression causes a fixed dilated pupil; the swinging light dilation comes from reduced afferent input from the optic nerve.
The ciliary ganglion has degenerated
Ciliary ganglion degeneration causes Adie's tonic pupil; the swinging light dilation comes from reduced afferent input.
The afferent stimulus on that side is reduced
Correct — the reduced afferent stimulus reduces the efferent signals to both pupils, so a net dilation occurs.
The affected pupil is pharmacologically blocked
Pharmacologic sphincter block is a cause of a dilated pupil, but the swinging light dilation comes from reduced afferent input.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 77

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Deep eye pain is associated with which condition?
opts: Allergic conjunctivitis
Allergy shows itching and excessive tearing rather than deep pain, which is linked to acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Corneal abrasion
A corneal abrasion is a surface injury that feels better with topical anesthetic; deep pain points to acute narrow angle glaucoma.
Blepharitis
Blepharitis is a common lid inflammation linked to bacterial infection or atopic dermatitis; deep pain points to angle closure.
Acute narrow angle glaucoma
Correct — deep eye pain is linked to acute narrow angle glaucoma; pain from a deeper source is not relieved by topical anesthetic.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 12

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Which of these complaints should be referred to ophthalmology IMMEDIATELY?
opts: Hyphema
Hyphema is urgent, not emergent: it needs ophthalmology follow-up within one day or less.
Orbital cellulitis
Orbital cellulitis is urgent, not emergent: it needs ophthalmology follow-up within one day or less.
Corneal abrasion
A corneal abrasion is urgent, not emergent: it needs ophthalmology follow-up within one day or less.
Chemical burn
Correct — chemical burns are emergent and go to ophthalmology immediately, as do rupture and sudden vision loss.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 124

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Lateral sparseness of the eyebrows suggests what?
opts: Hypothyroidism
Correct — lateral sparseness of the eyebrows is the eyebrow finding associated with hypothyroidism.
Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is linked to lid lag, not eyebrow loss; lateral eyebrow sparseness suggests hypothyroidism.
Seborrheic dermatitis
Seborrheic dermatitis causes scaliness of the eyebrows; lateral sparseness suggests hypothyroidism.
Iron deficiency
Iron deficiency is not an eyebrow association; lateral sparseness of the eyebrows suggests hypothyroidism.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 27

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Besides Horner syndrome and the senile and congenital forms, which causes of ptosis remain?
opts: Myasthenia gravis, oculomotor nerve damage
Correct — ptosis also comes from myasthenia gravis and oculomotor nerve damage, alongside Horner syndrome's sympathetic loss.
Bell palsy, trigeminal neuralgia and stroke
None of these is a ptosis cause; drooping of the upper lid comes from myasthenia gravis or oculomotor nerve damage.
Thyroid eye disease, orbital cellulitis and orbital tumor
Orbital disease such as cellulitis or tumor causes proptosis, not ptosis; ptosis comes from myasthenia gravis or third nerve damage.
Blepharitis, chalazion and dermatochalasis
Lid lesions such as a chalazion are not ptosis causes; the remaining causes are myasthenia gravis and oculomotor nerve damage.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 29

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Which pair of diagnoses must be differentiated because the latter can lead to death?
opts: Episcleritis from scleritis
Nodular episcleritis goes with rheumatoid arthritis and lupus; the pair that matters because one can kill is preseptal versus orbital cellulitis.
Cataract from glaucoma
Simple glaucoma and cataract both cause gradual painless loss; the pair that matters because one can kill is preseptal versus orbital cellulitis.
Hordeolum from chalazion
A hordeolum is a painful lid-margin infection and a chalazion a painless nodule; the pair that matters is preseptal versus orbital cellulitis.
Preseptal from orbital cellulitis
Correct — preseptal cellulitis must be told apart from orbital cellulitis, because orbital cellulitis can lead to death.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: In acute glaucoma, what is the pupil like?
opts: May be small and, with time, irregular
A small pupil that may become irregular is acute iritis; in acute glaucoma the pupil is dilated and fixed.
Not affected unless iritis develops
A pupil spared unless iritis develops is corneal injury or infection; in acute glaucoma it is dilated and fixed.
Dilated and fixed
Correct — acute glaucoma gives a dilated, fixed pupil, with a steamy cornea and an acute rise in intraocular pressure.
Not affected
An unaffected pupil belongs to conjunctivitis and subconjunctival hemorrhage; in acute glaucoma it is dilated and fixed.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Which examination comes FIRST in the suggested order?
opts: Direct ophthalmoscopy
Direct ophthalmoscopy comes last, among the special tests with the slit lamp and ocular pressure; inspection comes first.
Ocular pressure
Ocular pressure is a special test near the end, done only if it can be measured accurately and safely; inspection comes first.
Inspection
Correct — the suggested order begins with inspection, then the external examination, before acuity and fields.
Visual acuity
Visual acuity follows inspection and the external examination of the cornea, lens and pupils.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: What should you do if nystagmus is seen on lateral gaze?
opts: Refer immediately regardless
A few beats on lateral gaze are normal, so first bring the finger back into binocular vision and see if it persists.
Measure the intraocular pressure
Pressure has no role here; bring the finger back into binocular vision and consider neurologic disease if nystagmus persists.
Bring the finger back into binocular vision
Correct — bring the finger back into binocular vision; nystagmus that persists there suggests a neurologic condition.
Repeat the whole test with the other eye covered
Covering an eye is not the step; bring the finger back into the binocular field and see whether the nystagmus persists.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 63

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: When should the lacrimal sac compression test be avoided?
opts: If the patient has previously had cataract surgery on that eye
Cataract surgery in the elderly is a reason not to dilate the pupils, not to skip this test; avoid it if the area is inflamed.
If the patient is over sixty-five
Age is no reason to avoid it; the lacrimal sac compression test is avoided when the area is significantly inflamed or tender.
If the area is significantly inflamed or tender
Correct — the lacrimal sac compression test is avoided if the area is significantly inflamed or tender.
If the patient wears contact lenses
Contact lens wear is no reason to avoid it; the test is avoided only when the area is significantly inflamed or tender.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 38

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: A BLUE sclera indicates what?
opts: Long-term steroid use
Steroid use is a cataract risk factor, not a cause of scleral color; a blue sclera suggests osteogenesis imperfecta.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Correct — a blue sclera is the scleral color seen in osteogenesis imperfecta.
Liver disease
Liver disease gives a yellow sclera through jaundice; a blue sclera is seen in osteogenesis imperfecta.
Thyroid eye disease
Thyroid eye disease causes proptosis and lid lag, not scleral color; a blue sclera suggests osteogenesis imperfecta.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 43

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: Eye pain with PHOTOPHOBIA suggests what?
opts: Inflammation of the iris
Correct — eye pain accompanied by photophobia is the pairing for inflammation of the iris.
Optic neuritis
Optic neuritis causes pain on eye motion; eye pain with photophobia suggests inflammation of the iris.
Temporal arteritis
Temporal arteritis pairs eye pain with temporal pain; photophobia suggests inflammation of the iris.
Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis pairs eye pain with a gritty feeling; photophobia suggests inflammation of the iris.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 17

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: What does the cover-uncover test reveal?
opts: A slight muscle imbalance not otherwise seen
Correct — the cover-uncover test may reveal a slight muscle imbalance not otherwise seen.
An afferent pupillary defect of the optic nerve
An afferent pupillary defect is found with the swinging light test; cover-uncover reveals slight muscle imbalance.
A refractive error
Refractive error is shown by pinhole testing; the cover-uncover test reveals slight muscle imbalance.
A field defect
Field defects are found by confrontation testing; the cover-uncover test reveals slight muscle imbalance.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 67

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: In acute glaucoma, what is the cornea like?
opts: Steamy and cloudy
Correct — acute glaucoma makes the cornea steamy and cloudy, alongside a dilated fixed pupil and severe deep pain.
Clear
A clear cornea belongs to conjunctivitis and subconjunctival hemorrhage; acute glaucoma makes it steamy and cloudy.
Clear or slightly clouded
Clear or slightly clouded is the cornea of acute iritis; acute glaucoma makes it steamy and cloudy.
Changes depending on the cause
A cornea that changes with the cause is corneal injury or infection; acute glaucoma makes it steamy and cloudy.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 48 (image only)

set2.io: Instructional Objectives — Advanced Ocular Medical History and Examination
set2.q: What is the first step in everting the upper lid to search for a foreign body?
opts: Ask the patient to look up and relax, then pull the upper lid directly upward
The patient looks down, not up, and the lashes are pulled gently down and forward rather than straight upward.
Press on the globe itself to push the lid outward
You never press on the eyeball itself; the patient looks down and the lid is turned over a stick above the tarsal plate.
Use a cotton swab placed at the lid margin itself
The stick goes at least 1 cm above the lid margin, at the upper border of the tarsal plate, after the patient looks down.
Ask the patient to look down and relax
Correct — the patient looks down and relaxes; then the lashes are pulled down and forward over a stick placed 1 cm above the margin.
set2.cite: PD II Advanced Exam Ocular Lecture - Beck.pptx, Slide 42
